editorial:
Tarzan the Ape Man was released by MGM (Loew's Inc.) in the US on April 2, 1932, after a New York premiere on March 22. W.S. Van Dyke directed it. It was Johnny Weissmuller's first of 12 Tarzan films and brought the Tarzan yell to the screen. It cost $652,675 and earned $2.54 million, and it led to five sequels pairing Weissmuller with Maureen O'Sullivan between 1934 and 1942.

The rights trap is that a 1932 film is not free by default. Its status turns on whether MGM renewed the copyright in 1959-1961. I could not check that renewal record, so the print stays unresolved. The 1912 Burroughs novel it adapts is a separate work with a separate term. Tarzan character and franchise marks can outlive any copyright, and I have not confirmed who holds them. Do the renewal search yourself before reusing any footage.
faq: Is Tarzan the Ape Man (1932) in the public domain?

Unconfirmed. As a 1932 film it is free only if it was published without notice or its copyright was not renewed in 1959-1961. I could not complete that renewal check, so treat it as protected until a Copyright Office or Stanford renewal record shows otherwise.
Does the 1912 source novel make the film free to use?
No. The 1912 novel Tarzan of the Apes is a separate work with its own term. The 1932 film is a separate work, and any Tarzan trademarks are a third layer.
